title: "Owner of the Day of Judgment"
hook: a day when every account is settled, held by the one just named merciful
carry: the account is in kind hands
tomorrow: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help"

segments.voice: Yesterday: rahma, mercy, named twice in a row. Your line was mercy twice before anything else. Did you find two kind things to say before you judged something? Day nine.

Think of the good things you've done that nobody saw. The dishes you washed that weren't yours. The angry text you never sent. The night you sat up with someone and never mentioned it again. Most of it vanishes. Nobody keeps score of the quiet stuff. Now think of the other side too: the things you got away with, the ones that still bother you at two in the morning. Today's verse says both columns are kept. It sounds, at first, like a warning dropped into the middle of a mercy prayer. Listen to where it sits.
screen: `THE GOOD NOBODY SAW.` → `THE THINGS YOU GOT AWAY WITH.` → `BOTH COLUMNS ARE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Verse four, in Pickthall's words: “Owner of the Day of Judgment.” In Arabic, maliki yawmi d-din. Today's word is the day itself: yawm ad-din. Yawm is day. And din, translated judgment, is also the everyday Arabic word for religion, a way of life. At its root it carries the sense of a debt coming due, an account settled. So this is the day when every account is squared, both columns, the unseen good and the unfinished wrong. Two details for the curious. The Qur'an has more than one accepted way of being recited, and in some that first word is maalik, owner, the reading Pickthall translates. In others it's malik, king. Both are accepted. Now, where it sits. Two verses of praise and mercy, the Beneficent, the Merciful, and only then the Day. The same one who was just named merciful, twice, is the one who holds the account. Scholars have read that order as the point: the reckoning isn't in the hands of a stranger, or an enemy, or a machine. It's held by mercy. And the Day is the promise that nothing quiet is lost: the dishes, the unsent message, the night beside someone. In the conversation hadith recorded by Muslim, God answers this verse too: My servant has glorified Me. Some narrations add: My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me. That's the feeling underneath. Not dread. Handing the account over. Four verses down, three to go. And tomorrow, the prayer turns around.
screen: `YAWM AD-DIN — THE DAY OF THE ACCOUNT.` · `DIN — A DEBT COMING DUE.` · `MAALIK OR MALIK — BOTH ACCEPTED.` · `HELD BY THE ONE NAMED MERCIFUL.` · then, large: `THE ACCOUNT IS IN KIND HANDS.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Think of one good thing you did that nobody noticed. Let it be small. Hold it, and let it be enough that it happened. Then think of one thing you'd like to settle well, an apology, a debt, a promise. Don't solve it. Just set it down in front of you, honestly. If you pray, you can let the Arabic sit with both: maliki yawmi d-din. The bell holds the time.
Yawm ad-din. The Day of Judgment, the day every account is settled, held by the one just named merciful. Ninth word.
Your line: the account is in kind hands. Today, do one good thing nobody will see, and don't mention it to anyone. Day nine.

screen: `DAY 9 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "THEE (ALONE) WE WORSHIP; THEE (ALONE) WE ASK FOR HELP."`

howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in every unit of every prayer. Belief in the Last Day is one of the articles of faith in Islam, and many Muslims describe it as the reason no good deed, however small or hidden, is wasted.

fork.setup: in the conversation hadith, someone praying says: Owner of the Day of Judgment. how does God answer?
fork.reveal: My servant has glorified Me; some narrations add: My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me. not a threat, a handing-over.

original.note: Arabic: the Day of Judgment. din also means religion, a way of life, and carries the sense of a debt coming due.

trapdoor: what you thought: the scary verse in the middle.
what it means: a day when every account is settled, held by the one named merciful twice before it.
what a scholar hears: two accepted readings, maaliki (owner) and maliki (king); din from a root of debt and requital, and the verse is the hinge between praise (verses 2–3) and address (verse 5).

sources.quoted: Owner of the Day of Judgment

notes: The readings maalik / malik: both are among the accepted canonical readings (e.g. Hafs reads maaliki; Warsh reads maliki). Confirm the framing.
The addition 'My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me' appears in some narrations of the Muslim 395 hadith; confirm before keeping it.
Din glossed as judgment, religion and a debt coming due (requital): a standard lexical note; confirm.
